openers.chibanian-age: The age we still live in, magnetically speaking, began when Earth's field last reversed, ending the Matuyama chron and opening the Brunhes. By then the ice ages had settled into a new rhythm, and the Mid-Pleistocene Transition was complete by about 700,000 years ago. Giants were changing too: gomphotheres vanished from Africa and Eurasia, and the last clawed chalicotheres lived on only into this stretch of time. In California a VEI 7 eruption poured out about 600 km³ of rock, while lava flows dammed the Colorado River again and again. On the human side, hand axes reached Europe, small hominins lived on Flores, and the lines leading to Neanderthals and Denisovans parted about 640,000 years ago.

chib-001.title: The Brunhes–Matuyama reversal, Earth's last magnetic flip
chib-001.text: About 774,000 years ago, a compass needle would have swung around to point the way it points today. Earth's magnetic field last reversed then, ending the Matuyama chron, known as C1r, and opening the present Brunhes chron, C1n. Nobody knows quite how long the flip took. Estimates range from within a single human lifetime to several thousand years, or about 22,000 years. Part of the confusion is local. The apparent length of the flip at any one site can vary tenfold with geomagnetic latitude and local quirks of the field. Because it shows up worldwide in rock, the reversal is a precious marker. It is a standard tie-point for dating ocean sediment cores and volcanic rocks. In 2020 it was ratified as the golden spike, the GSSP, for the base of the Chibanian Stage, at the Chiba section in Japan.

chib-003.title: A turnover of mammals at the Middle Pleistocene
chib-003.text: As the Early Pleistocene gave way to the Middle, the cast of big mammals reshuffled. Sinomastodon died out in East Asia, and with it gomphotheres vanished from Africa and Eurasia, though they survived in the Americas into the Late Pleistocene. Many European carnivores died out, including the giant hyena Pachycrocuta. True horses migrated from North America into Eurasia. In Europe the mammoth Mammuthus meridionalis gave way to the Asian steppe mammoth, Mammuthus trogontherii. Out of Africa came Palaeoloxodon, including the first straight-tusked elephants, Palaeoloxodon antiquus.

chib-002.title: The last chalicotheres, horses with claws
chib-002.text: Imagine a relative of horses that walked on claws. The chalicotheres, or Ancylopoda, were clawed perissodactyls, the group of hoofed mammals that includes horses and rhinos. Their lineage lasted from the Eocene into the Middle Pleistocene. Sometime in that later stretch, between 774,000 and 129,000 years ago, the last of them disappeared.

chib-004.title: The Bishop Tuff eruption opens Long Valley Caldera
chib-004.text: About 760,000 years ago, eastern California exploded. A VEI 7 eruption released about 600 km³ of material, which cooled into a rock called the Bishop Tuff. Pyroclastic flows, avalanches of scorching gas and ash, burned and buried thousands of square miles. Ash blanketed much of the western United States. With its magma chamber drained, the ground above collapsed. The hole left behind, Long Valley Caldera, measures about 32 by 18 km and is one of the largest calderas on Earth.

chib-005.title: Lava dams choke the Colorado in the Grand Canyon
chib-005.text: Lava poured into the Grand Canyon more than 150 times. Between 725,000 and 100,000 years ago these basalt flows dammed the Colorado River at least 13 times. Each dam formed in a matter of weeks. Some stood up to 610 m high and 138 km long. How long they held back lakes behind them is still debated.

chib-007.title: The 100,000-year ice-age rhythm takes hold
chib-007.text: By about 700,000 years ago, Earth's climate had settled into the beat it still keeps. The Mid-Pleistocene Transition, under way since about 1.25 million years ago, was complete. Before it, ice ages came and went in cycles of about 41,000 years. Afterwards they followed lopsided, high-amplitude cycles averaging 100,000 years. Ice built up slowly over long cold spells, then melted fast, so the climate swings became more extreme. The warm spells changed too. Interglacials after the transition had more carbon dioxide in the air than those before it. The ice sheets of the new cycles locked up enormous amounts of water. Since about 600,000 years ago, six major glacial periods have lowered sea level by up to 120 m. Each time, the shallow edges of the continents were laid bare as dry land.

chib-008.title: Acheulean hand axes arrive in Europe
chib-008.text: About 700,000 years ago, typical Acheulean bifaces appeared in Europe. These are hand axes, stones flaked on both faces into a teardrop shape. Their sudden arrival has been argued to reflect influence from Africa rather than purely local invention. Late Acheulean culture, usually linked to the spread of {{ref:chib-017}}, reached across Europe and Africa by the beginning of the Middle Pleistocene.

chib-009.title: Tiny ancestors of the Flores 'hobbit'
chib-009.text: Small people were already small 700,000 years ago. Teeth and a partial jaw found at Mata Menge on Flores come from hominins thought to be ancestors of Homo floresiensis. They were as small as, or smaller than, the much later remains from Liang Bua. The species' small size therefore stayed stable for hundreds of thousands of years.

chib-010.title: A 'ghost' lineage splits from modern humans
chib-010.text: Some living Africans carry DNA from a people no one has ever found. An archaic hominin population broke away from the modern human lineage around 700,000 years ago. No fossils of it are known, which is why it is called a ghost lineage. About 35,000 years ago its DNA entered some sub-Saharan hunter-gatherer groups, such as the Biaka and the San.

chib-011.title: The Eridanos, a lost river of Europe, dies
chib-011.text: At its height about 2 million years ago, a great river ran some 2,700 km from Lapland across the Baltic region to a vast delta in western Europe. This was the Eridanos. Repeated Scandinavian ice caps destroyed its source area and gouged out the basin where the Baltic Sea later formed. During the first glacial stage of the Cromerian Complex, around 700,000 years ago, its deposits in the Netherlands stopped building up, and the Eridanos was gone.

chib-012.title: MIS 16, the Don Glaciation
chib-012.text: Few ice ages locked up as much water as this one. Marine Isotope Stage 16, a cold stage named from chemical signals in seafloor shells, ran from about 676,000 to 621,000 years ago. It was one of the two most extreme Quaternary glaciations by global ice volume, on par with MIS 12. Oddly, the oceans were only about as cold as in the neighboring glacials MIS 14 and MIS 18. On the East European Plain, the Don ice sheet reached the middle and lower Don basin at about 50° N, its greatest extent there.

chib-013.title: Neanderthals and Denisovans go separate ways
chib-013.text: Two of our closest cousins parted about 640,000 years ago, judging by genetic distances. Denisovans and Neanderthals then went their own ways. Their nuclear DNA shows they stayed closer to each other than either was to modern humans. {{ref:chib-017}} is usually considered the direct ancestor of both.

chib-014.title: The Lava Creek supereruption at Yellowstone
chib-014.text: About 631,000 years ago, Yellowstone tore itself open. Its third cycle peaked in a climactic eruption that produced the Lava Creek Tuff and created the present Yellowstone Caldera. Rated VEI 8, the top of the scale, it ejected more than 1,000 km³ of rock, dust and volcanic ash. Debris up to two meters deep covered a large part of North America, and the ash bed spread over 3 to 4 million km². The blast capped several hundred thousand years of rhyolitic volcanism, the explosive kind fed by sticky, silica-rich magma. It struck near the shift from the glacial MIS 16 to the interglacial MIS 15. Such events are rare on a human scale but common on a geological one. Eruptions this size happen somewhere on Earth about every 50,000 to 100,000 years.

chib-015.title: The Rockland eruption at Lassen
chib-015.text: About 610,000 years ago, the Lassen area of California blew out more than 130 km³ of rhyolite magma. Huge pyroclastic flows raced across the land, and an ash plume rose tens of kilometers high. Recent studies put the Rockland ash at up to 326.7 km³, over twice the ash of the Mazama eruption.

chib-016.title: The Great Barrier Reef builds its first full reefs
chib-016.text: The Great Barrier Reef is younger than it looks. Coral skeleton deposits on the Great Barrier Reef date back about half a million years. The earliest evidence of complete reef structures there is a little older, about 600,000 years.

chib-017.title: Homo heidelbergensis, the muddle in the middle
chib-017.text: About 600,000 years ago in Africa, a new kind of human evolved from Homo erectus. Homo heidelbergensis is known from fossils of the MIS 15 interglacial, between 621,000 and 563,000 years ago, including Heidelberg Man and the Bodo cranium. It was the likely ancestor of Denisovans and Neanderthals, and perhaps of modern humans too. Some scholars place the first symbolic communication with this species. Yet it is a controversial, poorly defined species, and its classification is disputed. The tangle of Middle Pleistocene human forms is nicknamed the 'muddle in the middle'.

chib-019.title: Today's Cascade volcanoes begin to grow
chib-019.text: The snowy volcanoes of the Pacific Northwest are young. About half a million years ago an older generation of Cascade volcanoes died, and many of today's stratovolcanoes began to grow. Glacier Peak and Mount Shasta started about 600,000 years ago, along with Newberry Volcano and Mount Tehama. Rainier and Hood followed at 500,000 years, Adams at 450,000 and Mazama at 420,000.

chib-020.title: The woolly mammoth evolves in Siberia
chib-020.text: The woolly mammoth did not invent its cold tolerance from scratch. Siberian mammoths over a million years old already carried many of its genes for surviving cold. Its lineage began to diverge from the steppe mammoth, Mammuthus trogontherii, about 800,000 years ago. By around 600,000 to 500,000 years ago the woolly mammoth had evolved in Siberia. Molars with 26 ridges, its trademark grinding teeth, appeared about 400,000 years ago. Its genes spread to the Americas too. Columbian mammoths descend half from woolly mammoths and half from the Krestovka lineage, which interbred more than 420,000 years ago. Woolly mammoth numbers crashed around 280,000 years ago, then recovered.

chib-021.title: The Lonar crater in India's basalt
chib-021.text: In Maharashtra, a meteorite traveling at hypervelocity punched a crater 1.8 km wide and 150 m deep into the Deccan basalt. It holds India's only crater lake of meteoritic origin. Its age is uncertain. Argon–argon dating gives 570 ± 47 thousand years, far older than an earlier estimate of 52 ± 6 thousand years. That older figure is disputed, because argon left over from older rock may have made the crater look older than it is.

chib-022.title: Tautavel Man in the Arago Cave
chib-022.text: A limestone cave at Tautavel in France sheltered archaic humans for a very long time. People lived in the Caune de l'Arago from about 550,000 to 400,000 years ago. Almost all the human remains come from one layer, bed G, dated by uranium–thorium to 455,000 years ago. Outside, the landscape swung again and again between temperate forest and cold, dry, grassy steppe.

chib-023.title: Zigzags on a shell, possibly the first art
chib-023.text: Someone on Java scratched a geometric pattern into a freshwater mussel shell between 546,000 and 436,000 years ago. The Pseudodon shell from Trinil could be the earliest known art-making. The Homo erectus people at Trinil also made scrapers from such shells, possibly prying them open with shark teeth. They lived there between 540,000 and 430,000 years ago. That was late in a long occupation of Java that had begun at Sangiran 1.51 to 0.93 million years ago.

chib-024.title: MIS 13, a Cromerian warm spell
chib-024.text: Between about 524,000 and 474,000 years ago, Britain enjoyed a warm interglacial, MIS 13, late in the Cromerian. It followed the relatively mild glacial MIS 14 and came before the cold MIS 12. Forests of birch, pine and spruce opened it. Boxgrove then lay on the coast beneath chalk cliffs, where mudflats gave way to woodland and grassland.

chib-025.title: The first brown bears
chib-025.text: Brown bears are relative newcomers. The first ones appeared around half a million years ago, in the Middle Pleistocene.

chib-026.title: Homo heidelbergensis settles Europe
chib-026.text: Around 500,000 years ago, early humans often called Homo heidelbergensis came to Europe from Africa. Their descendants there eventually evolved into Neanderthals. Groups had already dispersed into Europe by 700,000 years ago, spreading Late Acheulean tools, and more permanent groups settled north of 45° N about then. They pushed north beyond the 50th parallel, to Boxgrove and Eartham Pit in England. Boxgrove in Sussex, about 500,000 years old, is the earliest site in Britain with fossils of Homo. Settlements became more permanent by then, and occupation grew much more frequent afterward.

chib-027.title: Lake Victoria and the White Nile take shape
chib-027.text: Around half a million years ago, Lake Victoria took roughly its modern shape. The plateau that holds East Africa's great lakes tilted north. Water began to drain, on and off, toward Egypt, roughly along the course of the modern White Nile. Ancient lakes formed where the Sudd swamps now lie.

chib-031.title: The Anglian–Elster glaciation buries northern Europe
chib-031.text: Ice spread across North Germany and much of Europe on a scale never seen there before. The Elster glaciation, called the Anglian in Britain, lasted from about 480,000 to 424,000 years ago. Globally it matched MIS 12, the stronger glacial of its era, which ranks with MIS 16 among the two largest Quaternary ice volumes. An ice sheet filled much of the North Sea. South of it lay a large lake of meltwater fed by the Rhine, Scheldt and Thames. Great Britain was widely glaciated, and the long, relatively warm Cromerian Complex came to an end.

chib-032.title: The mammoth steppe is born
chib-032.text: During the MIS 12 glacial, about 460,000 years ago, a new kind of landscape appeared. The steppe-tundra biome, also called the mammoth steppe, first emerged. It joined animals of the northern tundra with those of the Central Asian steppe into one community. Cold, dry grassland stretched where the two had once been separate. This biome was not fixed. It grew with every later glacial cycle and shrank in each warm spell, again and again.

chib-033.title: A megaflood cuts Britain loose from France
chib-033.text: Britain became an island in a catastrophe. During the Anglian glaciation, about 450,000 years ago, an ice dam to the north backed river water into a vast lake in the southern North Sea. The lake was held in by a chalk ridge running from the Weald in England to Artois in France. Then the lake broke through. It was the first of two megafloods that cut through this Weald–Artois Anticline. The flood diverted the Rhine into the English Channel. Sonar shows deeply gouged channels and streamlined islands on the seabed. The land bridge between Britain and France was broken, though links returned whenever sea level fell low.

chib-034.title: Early Neanderthals in the Pit of Bones
chib-034.text: A deep pit in the Atapuerca hills of Spain holds bones that kept their DNA for some 430,000 years. The hominins of Sima de los Huesos, the 'Pit of Bones', were early members of the Neanderthal line. They yield the oldest known human DNA. Their anatomy suggests many Neanderthal traits had already evolved by the middle of the Middle Pleistocene. They probably lived through one of the coldest glacial phases of the last million years, which dried out Iberia.

chib-036.title: MIS 11, the super-interglacial
chib-036.text: Between about 424,000 and 374,000 years ago, Earth went through an unusually long, warm spell. MIS 11 was the longest and warmest interglacial of the last 500,000 years, possibly twice as long as the others. It began with the highest-amplitude deglacial warming of the last 5 million years. The north felt it most. South Greenland nearly lost its ice entirely around 410,000 to 400,000 years ago, adding 4.5 to 6 m to sea level. High-latitude seas were warm and the thermohaline circulation, the deep ocean conveyor driven by heat and salt, ran strong. Sea level stood higher than today, and coral reefs expanded. The same warm spell carries different names on land. It is the Hoxnian in Britain, the Holsteinian in Central Europe and the Yarmouthian in North America. Swanscombe Man, a fossil human from England, dates from it.

chib-037.title: The Clactonian tool industry
chib-037.text: From about 400,000 years ago, Homo heidelbergensis developed a tool industry of its own, the Clactonian.

chib-038.title: The first modern grey wolves
chib-038.text: The earliest specimens of the modern grey wolf date to around 400,000 years ago, and possibly as early as 1 million years ago. At first they were no bigger than dholes, Asian wild dogs. Between 400,000 and 300,000 years ago the two were similar in size, but wolves were slowly growing larger.

chib-039.title: The first polar bears
chib-039.text: Polar bears are among the younger large mammals. The first of them appeared about 400,000 years ago, during the Middle Pleistocene.

chib-040.title: Humans learn to keep fire for good
chib-040.text: Fire had flickered in the human story for a long time, but only in scattered sparks. About 400,000 years ago, reliable evidence of regular fire use appears in the archaeological record. Before that, traces are sparse. The change may mark the true domestication of fire, with people able to start it at will. Or it may simply reflect better ways of keeping fires alight. The oldest definite fire-making comes from a Neanderthal site in eastern England, about 400,000 years old. It left burnt soil, handaxes cracked by heat and pyrite, a mineral struck to make sparks. European caves show no regular fire before 400,000 to 300,000 years ago. Good evidence follows the MIS 9 interglacial, about 340,000 years ago. Fire became widespread in the Middle Paleolithic, and humans were cooking food by about 250,000 years ago.

chib-041.title: The Saale glaciation complex
chib-041.text: Northern Europe was buried by Scandinavian ice three times on a grand scale, and the Saale complex was the middle one. It spanned about 400,000 to 130,000 years ago. Rather than one ice age, it holds several glacial cycles separated by warmer periods. It opens with the Fuhne cold phase and the Dömnitz interglacial. Its later part matches the global Penultimate Glacial Period. Britain's equivalent, the Wolstonian, lasted about 374,000 to 130,000 years ago. In the Alps, the Riss glaciation is paralleled by MIS 10, 8 and 6.
